hints: Notice that two separate tests must be passed here, both L and M must dissolve first, and then their ions must combine to make something insoluble.
Recall your key Group 2 solubility rules, most chlorides, nitrates and magnesium sulfate are soluble, but barium sulfate and barium carbonate are insoluble.
Think about swapping the ions to make new pairs, and look for the combination that gives insoluble barium sulfate as the white solid.
walkthrough:
**Check That L and M Are Both Soluble**

You are told L and M both dissolve in water, so we can immediately reject any pair containing an insoluble starting compound.

Remember: $\text{BaSO}_4$ and $\text{BaCO}_3$ are both insoluble in water.

**Check For A Precipitate On Mixing**

When two soluble salts mix, the ions swap partners. A white precipitate forms only if one of the new products is insoluble.

The classic test is:
$$\text{Ba}^{2+}(aq) + \text{SO}_4^{2-}(aq) \rightarrow \text{BaSO}_4(s)$$

**Apply To The Pairs**

Soluble $\text{BaCl}_2$ provides $\text{Ba}^{2+}$ and soluble $\text{MgSO}_4$ provides $\text{SO}_4^{2-}$.

On mixing:
$$\text{BaCl}_2(aq) + \text{MgSO}_4(aq) \rightarrow \text{BaSO}_4(s) + \text{MgCl}_2(aq)$$
This gives the observed white precipitate of barium sulfate, while the other soluble-soluble pair gives only soluble products.

options.A: Both barium chloride and magnesium sulfate are soluble, so the first condition is met. On mixing, Ba2+ meets SO4 2- to form insoluble white barium sulfate, BaSO4(s), leaving soluble magnesium chloride in solution. This perfectly matches the observation.
options.B: Barium sulfate is famously insoluble in water, so this pair fails the first statement that L and M are both soluble. You cannot make a solution of BaSO4 to mix in the first place.
options.C: Both barium nitrate, Ba(NO3)2, and magnesium chloride, MgCl2, are soluble, but swapping ions gives BaCl2 and Mg(NO3)2 which are also both soluble. No insoluble product forms, so no precipitate would be seen.
options.D: Barium carbonate, BaCO3, is insoluble in water, so this pair fails the soluble starting material condition. It is a common trap to think of carbonate as the precipitate, but it cannot be L or M here because it would not dissolve.
